analysis.one_liner: Sets patient-protection rules for employer health plans, creates small-business health purchasing pools, and caps medical lawsuit damages.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 21 Republican cosponsors including the Speaker, but never received a hearing or vote in any of its four assigned committees before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write federal rules for employer health plans: doctors could not be gagged from advising patients, emergency care would be covered without pre-approval when a reasonable person would seek it, women could see an OB-GYN directly, plans would have to disclose coverage limits and drug formulary changes, and denied claims would go through fast-track appeals with outside medical review and fines for plans that ignore review decisions. It would also let trade associations and chambers of commerce sponsor health plans for small employers, expand tax-favored medical savings accounts, and impose a national limit on non-economic damages in medical lawsuits, shielding FDA-approved drug and device makers from punitive damages.
analysis.who_benefits: People covered by employer health plans gain guaranteed access to emergency care and specialists, honest medical advice from their doctors, clear plan disclosures, and a faster appeal process with outside medical experts and penalties for plans that deny care against an expert's recommendation. Small employers gain new lower-cost group-purchasing options. Physicians and insurers gain national limits on malpractice lawsuit damages.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits health plans from restricting what a doctor or other health professional may tell a patient about their condition or treatment options.

Requires plans to cover emergency room screening without preauthorization and without network limits whenever a prudent layperson would judge it necessary, and lets patients see an OB-GYN or pediatric specialist without a referral.

Requires plans to disclose covered and excluded benefits, utilization-review rules, formularies, and quality data, and to give 30 days' advance notice before dropping a drug used for a chronic illness from the formulary.

Sets deadlines for coverage decisions (72 hours for emergencies), requires physician review of medical-necessity denials, creates independent external review, and lets patients sue a plan fiduciary for civil penalties of up to $500 a day ($1,000 for bad faith, capped at $250,000) plus attorney's fees for ignoring a favorable outside review, with expedited court access when delay risks irreparable harm to health.

Lets certified trade, professional, and industry associations and chambers of commerce sponsor association health plans for small employers, with rules barring rate variation by claims experience or business type, and creates nonprofit 'HealthMarts' purchasing pools for small employers with portability of coverage between jobs.
Removes the existing cap on the number of medical savings accounts and lets all employers offer them.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans bear new coverage mandates, disclosure duties, appeal deadlines, outside review, and fines. Drug and device makers, physicians, and medical malpractice insurers gain protection from punitive damages but face new liability for ignoring external review recommendations. Small employers purchasing through the new pools gain, while states lose some regulatory authority over those plans. Patients would trade broader access to the courts for the bill's limited internal and external appeal remedies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, drug makers, and trial lawyers

drawbacks.text: The bill caps non-economic damages in medical liability cases nationwide and overrides differing state laws, so a patient with severe but non-economic injuries could recover far less than under many state laws.
It bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices, removing a deterrent even where state law would have allowed it.

For most denied-coverage disputes the only path to court runs through the bill's internal and external review process, and a plan's decision on medical necessity is reviewed against the plan's own terms; the sweeping remedies are triggered mainly when a plan defies an external reviewer's recommendation, so patients suing for other wrongs would remain largely inside the ERISA framework's limits.

Association health plans and HealthMarts are exempt from certain state insurance laws, which critics of such arrangements have long argued can draw healthier groups out of state-regulated markets and raise costs for those who remain; the bill does include solvency, surplus, and anti-discrimination rules to limit that risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are genuine and specific: gag-clause bans, prudent-layperson emergency coverage, direct OB-GYN and pediatric access, real deadlines, and outside review with teeth for plans that defy it. But the bill's lawsuit provisions are a significant trade-off — they cap damages nationally, immunize FDA-approved products from punitive damages, and channel most coverage disputes into plan-run review rather than court. It is a package that gives patients meaningful process protections while leaving insurers' broad ERISA litigation shield largely intact, and its small-business purchasing pools come with solvency rules but weaken state oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees and three health subcommittees within a month of introduction, then never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Bilirakis introduced the Patient Protection Act of 1999 on February 2, 1999, with 12 original cosponsors including Speaker Dennis Hastert.
The same day, the House referred it to the Commerce Committee and additionally to the Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees.
In February 1999 it was referred to the Health subcommittees of those committees, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill's cosponsors numbered 20, all Republicans, in addition to the sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers kept the status quo: no new federal coverage mandates, disclosure duties, external review, or liability penalties took effect from this bill. Patients gained nothing from it, and this bill also died before competing patient-protection proposals in the same Congress became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers keeping the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would impose new coverage mandates, disclosure duties, appeal deadlines, independent external review, and fines on insurers, but it would also keep most coverage disputes out of court and preserve the ERISA framework that shields employer plans from broad lawsuits, while the tort title caps malpractice exposure industry-wide.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug and medical device makers
industries.note: The bill bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices, a protection that comes directly out of injured patients' potential recoveries.
National limits on non-economic damages and shared-fault rules reduce malpractice exposure, while the gag-clause ban and specialist-access rules limit plans' control over physician advice.

industries.industry: Trade associations and chambers of commerce
industries.note: The bill lets associations sponsor certified health plans for small employers under federal rather than full state regulation, a new business line, though with solvency and anti-discrimination conditions attached.
Damage caps, preemption of state liability laws, and limits on punitive damages shrink the pool of health-care litigation and fee recoveries.
